@@137280675 <h> Can Australia ever win Eurovision ? Yes , but do we really need to ? <p> Soaring into the sky in a shower of fire and golden sunlight , Australian singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem delivered a career-defining performance that became the talk of Eurovision . To be fair , it was a tough field , but even competition-hardened Eurovision expert Graham Norton tipped it as this year 's competition-winning performance . <p> In the end , however , Goodrem walked away in fourth place , after Eurovision 's hectic TV audience-voting phase upended the scoreboard , burying favourites France , Italy and Greece , elevating Israel and Romania to second and third place , and catapulting Bulgaria into an unassailable lead that nobody , not even sun goddess Delta Goodrem , could match . <p> Loading <p> That is the nature of Eurovision . It 's as crazy and colourful on the scoreboard as it is on the stage . In 2016 , Dami Im faced a similar battle . She delivered a stunning performance but the competition ended in a brutal twist that pushed her to second place . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- she literally took flight -- but she too was pushed into ninth place , after an unfairly harsh jury vote . <p> As the Australian delegation packs its bags tonight in Vienna preparing to head home , the mood is upbeat . Goodrem herself is thrilled with the outcome . And in truth , fourth place in a field of 35 , is a noble outcome . But it does leave us with a lingering question . Just what do we have to do to win the Eurovision Song Contest ? <p> Advertisement <p> The answer is not as simple as send an extraordinary singer and equip her with an extraordinary song . The Eurovision Song Contest is a Rubik 's Cube of diplomacy , old family ties and geopolitical ballet . You can spin it every which way but until you make the colours line up , you will never solve the puzzle . <p> Winning , of course , is a remote target in a busy shooting gallery . There are between 35 and 45 countries competing each year . This year the total was down because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tough . And in a less febrile political climate , the competition is even tougher . <p> In the process of brutal semi-finals , a dozen of those countries are culled . Only the biggest spenders in the European Broadcasting Union ( EBU ) -- the UK , Spain , Germany , France and Italy -- are guaranteed a berth in the grand final . ( Spain was one of the five countries absent this year . ) Even in the world of art , money talks a loud game . <p> On top of that Australia has some real competitive hurdles to overcome . The Eurovision scoring system is structured so that each country scores the others , and can not vote for its own artist and song . <p> Advertisement <p> But in a 70-year-old competition , laid over centuries of European geopolitics , alliances have risen and fallen , some now so deep that they are impossible to shift . Companies love recurring payments because they generate regular income and provide personal data they can monetise . Entire businesses are now devoted to " customer retention " . <p> Which is why the simple act of cancelling subscriptions feels closer to conducting a hostage negotiation . <p> Researchers like those at the consumer rights website Deceptive Patterns have identified techniques they have dubbed " roach motel " practices , named after a disposable cardboard insect trap marketed in the US in the 1980s that used bait and a sticky interior to lure insects inside with no chance of escape . <p> Check out anytime you like . But you can never leave . While signing up is simple , trying to cancel involves confusing trick questions , hidden or obscure menus or having to call a support line during business hours that , naturally @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a process specifically designed to wear down people who are already time-poor . Cynical and cunning ? Certainly . Regulatory authorities , busily tracking the Machiavellian practices of supermarkets and petrol conglomerates , should take a deeper look . <p> To be fair , the subscription economy did n't conquer the world through corporate trickery . Its success lies in the choice and flexibility it offers the consumer - access to information and entertainment unimaginable a decade ago . It 's also proven a lifesaver for many traditional businesses like the media ( you would n't be reading this now without the income generated by loyal subscribers ) . <p> Recurring payments , however , are a radical change for capitalism . In only a few years we have discarded the concept of ownership and accepted leasing as the bedrock of doing business . <p> We once bought LPs and CDs , displaying them on shelves like trophies . Now we rent access to 100 million songs and movies . Remember when you had to purchase software ? Now computers become obsolete unless we annually update with a subscription . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ longer requires the ability to persuade us once . The best sales technique is persuading us to forget we ever signed on in the first place . <p> That way they have us for life . <p> When cancelling feels like hostage negotiation <p> HAVE YOUR SAY : Have you experienced difficulties trying to cancel subscriptions ? Do you fear you subscribe to too many services ? Should the government clamp down on companies deliberately making it difficult to cancel ? @@137690855 <h> He was making a film about our shameful Nazi past -- then the present intervened <p> Dan Goldberg was close to finishing his SBS documentary The Hunt For Australia 's Last Nazis -- which he had thought was a story about " Australia 's shameful past " -- when the massacre at Bondi Beach happened . Suddenly and horrifically , he says , " the present and the past collided " . <p> Journalist and filmmaker Dan Goldberg 's film The Hunt For Australia 's Last Nazis is on SBS . SBS <p> By the time he got back to his film in early January , he had to work out how to handle what he calls " the elephant in the room " -- the events of December 14 , 2025 , when two men shot into the Chanukah by the Sea gathering at Bondi , leaving 15 people ( plus one of the gunmen ) dead , and another 40 injured . <p> " My first instinct was no , it 's a different story , it 's a different time , it 's a different place @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fresh , it 's too raw , it 's too confronting , " he says . ' " <p> Advertisement <p> Whatever the complexities of the ongoing conflict in Gaza and the Israeli government 's response to the October 2023 terror attack by Hamas , The Hunt For Australia 's Last Nazis does a tremendous job of giving voice to the sense of vulnerability Australian Jews have long felt in this country , and the very solid reasons they have for feeling it . <p> Goldberg 's film is principally concerned with the fact that among the displaced persons Australia accepted from Europe after World War II , more than 4000 of them were former Nazis . <p> Alleged Nazi mass murderer Konrad Kalejs , during the war and in 1997 . Reuters <p> " Thousands of people who had Nazi pasts were able to come through Australia 's flimsy security screening at this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concerned about building the nation than we were about people 's histories , " says academic Ruth Balint in the film . <p> Our immigration policy at the time was underpinned by the dual fear of communism and the perceived threat of Asian expansionist ambitions . <h> Related Article <p> " The mantra ' populate or perish ' really became Australia 's post-war immigration agenda , " Balint says . " This was a program built not on humanitarianism but on pragmatism . " <p> It was also built , adds historian Jayne Persian , on blatant racism . <p> " Immigration officers were explicitly told not to select Jews , " she says in the documentary . " Nationalities were ranked , with Balts people from the Baltic states of Latvia , Lithuania , Estonia at the top and Jews at the bottom . " <p> There was a profile Australia was selecting for , she adds . " They were supposed to fit in on Bondi Beach ... white , young , not Jewish , anti-communist . Hitler could not have done better . " <p> Advertisement <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when Attorney-General Sir Garfield Barwick told Parliament it was " time to close the chapter on war crimes ... it is , after all , 1961 " . <p> Australia thereby became the first country in the world to grant amnesty for war crimes , at the very same time as Adolf Eichmann was on trial in Israel for his role in the Holocaust . <p> The identification card Ivan Polyukhovich still possessed decades after arriving in Australia.SBS <p> It was n't until Bob Hawke set up the Special Investigations Unit in 1987 , with a brief to look into Nazi war criminals living in Australia , that this country appeared to think there was a principle at stake in reckoning with the past . By the time it closed in 1993 ( under Paul Keating ) , it had conducted 841 investigations , spent a truckload of money and recorded zero convictions . <p> Goldberg looks at three cases in some depth , of accused Nazi war criminals Konrad Kalejs , Karlis Ozols ( who became Australian chess champion in 1959 ) , and Ivan Polyukhovich , who , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , complete with swastika , in his possession . <p> Advertisement <p> Only Polyukhovich faced trial , and in July 1993 , despite testimony from eyewitnesses flown out from Ukraine who identified him as having killed people , he was acquitted . <p> The issue was never a lack of evidence , says Goldberg . It was that too much time had elapsed for those accounts to be beyond reasonable doubt , and any conviction to be deemed safe . And it was government policy that allowed that to happen . <p> Loading <p> " We just wanted to build the country , and to hell with whether people had blood on their hands , " he says . " They were young , they were fit , they were men -- and crucially , they were white men . " <p> Goldberg makes the point in the film that while Australia 's last Nazis have died , there are still war criminals among us from other spheres -- Rwanda , Sudan , the Balkans -- and they are just as likely to escape prosecution as were those who came @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ We 're one of the few Western countries that does n't have a permanent war crimes unit , " he says . " This is not just the past , it is the present . We ca n't allow history to repeat itself . It 's just criminal , and it 's on us . " <p> The Hunt For Australia 's Last Nazis is on SBSon Sunday , May 31 at 7:30pm and on SBS On Demand .
